t: A woman speaking, or a man?
p: Two manuscripts make the word "many" feminine, so the speaker is a woman; five make it masculine.

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscripts l and r
readings.en: that I (a woman) became many in children

readings.w: Manuscripts h, i, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote
readings.en: that I (a man) became many in children

why: The Plain English Translation keeps Swete's text. The English is the same either way; only the speaker changes. With the feminine, the voice is most naturally Jerusalem's (see the note on this verse); with the masculine, it is the poet's.

t: Spread out, or "may it go out"?
p: Three manuscripts say the wealth spread over the earth; four make it a wish, "may their wealth go out."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with the manuscripts Swete calls i, l and r
Manuscripts h, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote

why: The past tense fits the next lines, which describe what the rich did (1:5-8). Gray (1913) followed it and called the wish form an error.

a: They said they would never fall
t: "They will never fall" or "we will never fall"?
p: The manuscripts differ slightly in the verb; Gray guessed that the original said "we will never fall."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with the manuscripts Gray calls R and H
readings.plain: They said they would never fall

readings.w: Manuscript l, as Gray reports
readings.plain: They said they would never fall

why: The Plain English Translation keeps Swete's text; l's added particle does not change the sense.
b: Gray (1913) suggested that the original reading was pesōmen, "we shall never fall," the boast in the rich men's own words, and compared Psalm 30:6. No manuscript has it.

p: Most manuscripts say "his" (God's) glory; manuscript m says "her" glory, Jerusalem's.

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscripts h, i, l, p, r and v
Manuscript m, from Swete's footnote; adopted by von Gebhardt (1895), as Gray reports

why: Nearly all the manuscripts have "his." "Her" makes a smoother sense, since Jerusalem's beauty is the subject of 2:19-23, and that smoothness may be why a copyist wrote it.
b: Gray (1913) reported that von Gebhardt combined "her" with Hilgenfeld's conjecture "I have no pleasure in them" for the first half of the line, giving "I have no pleasure in them. / Her glorious beauty was set at naught before God." Gray found the conjecture attractive but thought it unbalanced the Hebrew lines.

p: Swete follows manuscript r, "Israel"; the other manuscripts have "Jerusalem."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscript r; the Syriac, as Gray reports
Manuscripts h, i, l, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote

why: Swete printed the reading of r, which the Syriac version supports (Gray). Von Gebhardt found r and the other family about equal in value (Gray). The sense hardly changes: Jerusalem stands for Israel throughout the psalm.
b: In the same line h and v read ἀπαγωγῇ, "leading away," for ἐπαγωγῇ, "bringing in," of the nations; Gray called h's form an error.

p: Three manuscripts say the body was tossed on the waves; four say it was destroyed.

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscripts i, l and r; the Syriac, as Gray reports
Manuscripts h, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote

why: The Plain English Translation keeps Swete's text, which has manuscripts i, l and r and, as Gray reports, the Syriac. Gray judged it the correct text. The two Greek words look alike, so one is a copying slip for the other.
b: Gray (1913) noted that the reading he took as correct, "borne hither and thither," is further from the literal truth of Pompey's end as Plutarch describes it than h's "destroyed." Plutarch says the murderers threw the body out of the boat and that it was later burned on the shore (Pompey 80).

p: Swete prints r's forms; the other manuscripts have the more usual spelling. The meaning is the same.

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscript r
Manuscripts c, h, i, l, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote

why: The Plain English Translation keeps Swete's text. "Destruction of the age" and "everlasting destruction" say the same thing.

t: His devout, or those with him?
p: Four manuscripts read "those who are with him" instead of "his devout."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscripts i, l, r and c
Manuscripts h, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote

why: "His devout" is the book's own term for the faithful (see the note on "devout"), and Gray (1913) followed it.

t: "A hymn and praise" or "a new hymn"?
p: Swete reads "a hymn and praise" (kai ainon); five manuscripts have "a new hymn" (kainon).

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscripts c, l and r
Manuscripts h, i, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote; followed by Gray (1913)

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text. The two readings differ by a single letter in Greek written without spaces (ΚΑΙΑΙΝΟΝ / ΚΑΙΝΟΝ). Gray preferred "new," which recalls the "new song" of the Psalms (Psalm 96:1; Psalm 149:1), and called the other reading an error. But a copyist who knew the Psalms could also have changed "and praise" to the familiar "new."

t: A good heart or a whole heart?
p: Two manuscripts read "good heart"; the rest have "whole heart."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscripts i and r; the Syriac, as Gray reports
Manuscripts c, h, l, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote

why: Gray (1913) preferred "good," which he understood as the Hebrew "glad heart" (as in Ruth 3:7 and Ecclesiastes 9:7), and compared James 5:13. "Whole heart" is the more common phrase in the Psalms, which makes it the likelier change.

p: Two manuscripts read "every godly man" (theion) instead of "devout" (hosion).

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscripts h, i, m, p, r and v
Manuscripts c and l, from Swete's footnote

why: "Devout" is the book's own term and has most of the manuscripts. Gray (1913) thought the Hebrew was chasid.

a: He has piled sins on top of sins
p: Three manuscripts have "he added"; four have "they added."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscripts i, l and r
readings.plain: He has piled sins on top of sins

readings.w: Manuscripts h, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote (Swete says the reading of c is not clear)
readings.plain: They have piled sins on top of sins

why: The Plain English Translation keeps Swete's text. The singular fits the portrait of "the sinner" in 3:11-13, and the next verse goes on with "he fell."

a: his fall is a bad one
p: Manuscript i reads "his seed is evil" instead of "his fall is evil."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with all the other manuscripts
readings.plain: his fall is a bad one

readings.w: Manuscript i, from Swete's footnote

why: "Fall" continues "He fell" and leads into "he will not rise." "Seed" in i is a slip between similar words.

p: Four manuscripts call this poem a "conversation"; three call it a "psalm," and m has no heading.

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscripts c, i, l and r
Manuscripts h, p and v, from Swete's footnote

why: "Conversation" is the rarer word and has the stronger support; a copyist was more likely to change it to the usual "psalm" than the reverse.
b: The Greek dialogē means a discussion or a speech addressed to someone, which fits a poem that begins by speaking directly to the unholy man (4:1). Gray (1913) translated "A Conversation of Solomon with the Men-pleasers." Manuscript i adds the number, "fourth."

t: The devout council, the council of the devout, or just "council"?
p: Manuscript i reads "the council of the devout"; h, m, p and v leave out "devout."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscripts c, l and r
Manuscript i, from Swete's footnote; the Syriac, as Gray reports
readings.en: in a council of the devout

readings.w: Manuscripts h, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote

why: The Plain English Translation follows Swete's text. Gray (1913) preferred i's "the council of the devout" as "the fuller and correcter phrase." The meaning is the same: the unholy man sits among the devout.

a: stands guilty with every kind of sinner
p: Swete follows r, "a variety of sinners"; all the other manuscripts have "a variety of sins."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscript r alone
readings.plain: stands guilty with every kind of sinner

readings.w: Manuscripts c, h, i, l, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote; followed by Gray (1913)
readings.plain: stands guilty of every kind of sin

why: The Plain English Translation keeps Swete's text, which here rests on one manuscript. The other reading is easier and has far more support, and Gray translated it ("guilty in respect of manifold sins"). The two Greek words differ by two letters. On either reading the judge is as guilty as those he condemns.

p: Swete follows r, "speaks only with deceit"; every other manuscript has "speaks the law with deceit."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscript r alone
Manuscripts c, h, i, l, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote; followed by Gray (1913)

why: The Plain English Translation keeps Swete's text. The two words (monon, nomon) are anagrams, and either could come from the other. "Speaking the law with deceit" has nearly all the manuscripts and fits the picture of a man who quotes the Law while breaking it (4:1-3). Gray translated it "who uttereth law guilefully" and reported von Gebhardt's view that the Hebrew may have meant "transgresses."

p: Swete follows r's plural, "may they fall away"; most manuscripts have "may he fall away."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscript r
Manuscripts c, h, i, l and v, from Swete's footnote (unaccented, as he prints it)
Manuscripts m and p, from Swete's footnote (unaccented, as he prints it)

why: The plural has no clear subject, which is why the Plain English Translation keeps it only as Swete's text. The singular, "may he fall," fits the curses around it, and Gray (1913) translated "Let him fail."
b: Swete's footnote also shows c, h, i, l, m, p and v adding "in dishonor" at the end of the line.

a: And let his house be lacking
t: An extra line in most manuscripts
p: Every manuscript but r has an extra line here: "May he come into his house empty-handed."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscript r alone
readings.plain: And let his house be lacking

readings.w: Manuscripts c, h, i, l, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote (unaccented as he prints it); followed by Gray (1913)
readings.orig: κενος χερσιν αυτου εισελθοι εις τον οικον αυτου, καὶ ἐλλιπὴς ὁ οἶκος αὐτοῦ
readings.en: may he come into his house with his hands empty, and lacking his house
readings.plain: May he come into his house empty-handed, and let his house be lacking

why: The Plain English Translation keeps Swete's text, which follows r. The extra line has all the other manuscripts, and Gray translated it ("Let him come home empty-handed to his house"). It gives verse 19 two lines like its neighbors, which supports it; a copyist's eye may have skipped from one "his house" to the next in r.

t: An extra "people" and a different order
p: Every manuscript but r puts the words in a different order and adds "of people" after "eyes."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscript r alone
readings.en: eyes may ravens peck out of those who play the hypocrite

readings.w: Manuscripts c, h, i, l, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote (as Swete abbreviates and prints it, unaccented)
readings.en: may ravens peck out the eyes of people (who play the hypocrite)

why: The Plain English Translation follows all the other manuscripts against r, as it does in the next verse. The sense hardly changes.

a: they have laid many people's houses waste
p: Swete follows r, which has the singular "he"; every other manuscript has the plural "they."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscript r alone
readings.orig: ὅτι ἠρήμωσεν οἴκους πολλοὺς ἀνθρώπων ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ καὶ ἐσκόρπισεν ἐπιθυμίᾳ
readings.en: for he laid waste many houses of people in dishonor and scattered (them) by desire
readings.plain: he has laid many people's houses waste

readings.w: Manuscripts c, h, i, l, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote (l and c also differ in the order of "many people"); translated by Gray (1913)
readings.orig: ὅτι ἠρήμωσαν οἴκους πολλοὺς ἀνθρώπων ἐν ἀτιμίᾳ καὶ ἐσκόρπισαν ἐν ἐπιθυμίᾳ
readings.en: for they laid waste many houses of people in dishonor and scattered (them) in desire
readings.plain: they have laid many people's houses waste

why: The Plain English Translation follows all the other manuscripts against r, and so departs from Swete's text. The plural has far more support, matches "the people-pleasers" and "the law-breakers" of 4:21, and leads into 4:24, "they did not remember God." r's singular looks like a carry-over from the singular man of 4:1-20. Gray translated the plural, "For they have laid waste many houses of men."

a: the refuge of the poor is kind and merciful
t: "The refuge is kind" or "you are kind"?
p: Swete follows r; the other manuscripts make it a direct address: "You are kind and merciful, the refuge of the poor."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscript r
readings.orig: εὔχρηστος καὶ ἐλεήμων ἡ καταφυγὴ τοῦ πτωχοῦ
readings.en: kind and merciful is the refuge of the poor
readings.plain: the refuge of the poor is kind and merciful

readings.w: Manuscripts c, h, i, l, m, p and v (with a small further difference in h, m, p and v), from Swete's footnote; followed by Gray (1913)
readings.orig: σὺ χρηστὸς καὶ ἐλεήμων ... ἡ καταφυγὴ τοῦ πτωχοῦ
readings.en: you are kind and merciful, the refuge of the poor
readings.plain: you are kind and merciful, the refuge of the poor

why: The Plain English Translation keeps Swete's text. The other reading has all the other manuscripts and fits the prayer, which speaks to God in the next line. The Greek letters of eu chrēstos and su chrēstos are close.

a: For no one will take plunder from a strong man.
t: A line missing in two manuscripts
p: Manuscripts c and l leave out this line; four others add "a man": "no man will take."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscripts i and r
readings.orig: οὐ γὰρ λήψεται σκῦλα παρὰ ἀνδρὸς δυνατοῦ.
readings.en: for he will not take spoils from a mighty man
readings.plain: For no one will take plunder from a strong man.

readings.w: Manuscripts h, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote
readings.orig: οὐ γὰρ λήψεται σκῦλα ἄνθρωπος παρὰ ἀνδρὸς δυνατοῦ.
readings.en: for a man will not take spoils from a mighty man
readings.plain: For no human being will take plunder from a strong man.

readings.w: Manuscripts c and l, from Swete's footnote

why: The line has most of the manuscripts and fits the argument of 5:5, so the Plain English Translation keeps it. Its loss in c and l is easy to explain if a copyist skipped a line.

p: Swete reads "in sparing"; h, m, p and v have "on a friend."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscripts c, l and r (i has a misspelling of the same word)
Manuscripts h, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote

why: "Sparing" sets up the contrast with God's rich, free gift (5:16). Gray (1913) thought "on a friend" arose from it by error.

p: Swete prints r's spelling, which read as written means "play"; manuscripts h, m, p and v spell "discipline."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscript r
readings.en: the whip of your play (as spelled); or a spelling of "discipline"

readings.w: Manuscripts h, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote; translated by Gray (1913)

why: The Plain English Translation follows h, m, p and v, as Gray did ("the rod of Thy chastening"), and so departs from Swete's printed form. Read as written, r's paidias is the word for play or a child's game, which makes no sense beside "yoke" and "whip." The two spellings sound alike, and the same spelling of "discipline" turns up elsewhere in Swete's text: at Isaiah 50:4 he prints glōssan paidias, where later hands in two of his manuscripts write paideias. So r very likely meant "discipline" too.
b: Swete's footnote also reports a third form, paideia, for another manuscript, and says that the reading of c is not clear. The sense of that form is the same as h, m, p and v's.

p: Two manuscripts read "judge her," that is, Jerusalem.

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscripts h, i, m, p, r and v
Manuscripts c and l, from Swete's footnote

why: Most manuscripts have "him." "Her" turns the line into the poet's fear for Jerusalem, which is what follows (8:4-6). See the note on this verse.

p: Three manuscripts have the sound going "into" (or "toward") Jerusalem; four have it "in" Jerusalem.

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscripts c, l and r
Manuscripts h, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote

why: The Plain English Translation keeps Swete's text. Gray (1913) also followed it ("a sound I hear (moving) towards Jerusalem") and thought the poet's distress fits best if he hears the armies advancing on the city as God's judgment on it (8:1-2). With "in," the poet hears the sound of judgment inside Jerusalem.

p: Three manuscripts have "his entry"; four have "their entry."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscripts i, l and r; the Syriac, as Gray reports
Manuscripts h, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote

why: The Plain English Translation keeps Swete's text, which Gray also followed. "His" is the conqueror of 8:16, whose entry the rulers prepare; "their" would mean his army.

p: Swete follows r's "he defiled"; the other manuscripts have "they defiled."

readings.w: Swete's printed text, with manuscript r
Manuscripts c, h, i, l, m, p and v, from Swete's footnote; followed by Gray (1913)

why: The Plain English Translation keeps Swete's text, but the plural has much more support and continues 8:25, "They did as their uncleanness led them." With the plural, Jerusalem's own people defiled it; with the singular, the conqueror did. Gray translated "They defiled Jerusalem."
